claim: Joseph Trumbull Stickney graduated Harvard A.B. 1895 and then spent the following years studying in Paris toward the Doctorat ès Lettres, awarded in 1903.
implication: Stickney is an American Harvard-trained near-peer already resident in Paris when Lovejoy arrived in 1898.
caution: Stickney left Harvard in 1895; Lovejoy entered Harvard graduate study in autumn 1895. Do not call them Harvard classmates or claim campus overlap.

claim: EPHE 1898-99 Religions de l'Inde names Stickney among the élèves titulaires, especially active in Foucher's Nyāya course, and says he himself took charge of a series of conferences on Sāṃkhya according to Garbe.
implication: Stickney occupies exactly the Sāṃkhya/Indian-philosophy problem field that intersects Lovejoy notebook 004.
caution: Same institution/year/problem is not personal contact.

claim: EPHE 1898-99 Sanskrit report says Stickney had solid knowledge of Sanskrit and Indian philosophy and participated constantly and very actively in Lévi's Bhagavad-Gītā conference; illness forced him to suspend a planned translation.
implication: An American student was in close Lévi textual work during Lovejoy's Paris year, providing a near-peer control for Lévi's teaching ecology.
caution: No evidence yet Lovejoy attended this conference or knew Stickney.

claim: EPHE 1899-1900 Religions de l'Inde names Stickney as élève titulaire and says he continued active work on Manu; Nyāya readings were added; his engagement persists beyond Lovejoy's year.
implication: Shows Stickney's Indianist participation was sustained, not a one-semester accident.
caution: Post-Lovejoy-year continuation does not establish prior social transmission.

claim: EPHE 1900-01 Sanskrit report explicitly states that 'en dehors de ces deux conférences' Lévi continued with Stickney the reading of the Bhagavad-Gītā left unfinished the previous year.
implication: Direct contemporary proof that Lévi conducted student-specific textual work outside the two regular conferences, an especially close institutional control for Wilson's report of Lovejoy's occasional private sacred-text readings.
caution: The location is not stated as Lévi's home; do not equate this supplementary reading with Lovejoy's reported home visits.

claim: The Lévi–Stickney Bhagavad-Gītā work ultimately became the posthumously published joint translation; BnF heritage material identifies Stickney as an American student whose work Lévi revised and enriched.
implication: Confirms the pedagogical relationship generated a durable textual product.
caution: Publication decades later should not be used to date each stage of the 1898-1900 collaboration more finely than EPHE reports allow.

claim: No current JHU ArchivesSpace or Harvard archival search produced a Lovejoy–Stickney correspondence or explicit personal link.
implication: Transmission hypothesis remains open but unproved.
caution: Name-index silence is not proof they never met; only no exposed archival component was found in this pass.

claim: Harvard holds Richard Sherman Nutt collection on Trumbull Stickney, HUM 420, 1892-1954, one document box, documenting later research into Stickney's life and influence.
implication: Potential reciprocal biographical source if we later need Stickney's Paris contacts/letters reproduced in Nutt's research.
caution: This is a later research collection, not Stickney's own fonds and not yet a positive Lovejoy component.
